name: Fly.io
tagline: Deploy one container on a self-owned host and expose operational limits clearly

pricing.notes: No stable monthly plan; pricing is usage based.

tiers.name: Pay as you go
tiers.limits: Per-second Machines billing; published 30-day examples include shared-cpu-1x at $2.02 for 256 MB, $3.32 for 512 MB, $5.92 for 1 GB and $11.11 for 2 GB.
tiers.notes: Additional published examples: shared-cpu-2x from $4.04/month, 4x from $8.08, 6x from $12.11 and 8x from $16.15, depending on RAM.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier for new organizations; legacy free allowances may survive only on older accounts
pricing.billingTerms: monthly pay as you go with per-second resource billing; no annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: RAM above the bundled amount is roughly $5/GB per 30 days; volumes, snapshots, dedicated IPs and network egress are separate. Optional support costs $29/month Standard, $199/month Premium or at least $2,500/month Enterprise; Fly Kubernetes starts at $75/cluster/month plus resources.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Fly.io, deploy one container on a self-owned host and expose operational limits clearly. The hard boundary is global edge compute, anycast networking, orchestration, volumes, and platform operations, plus infrastructure scale, operations, and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Deploy one container on a user-owned server, route domains, retain logs, perform backups, and expose operational limits clearly.
whatYouLose: global edge compute, anycast networking, orchestration, volumes, and platform operations
ongoingBurden: patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Fly.io because hosting products sell an operations team and failure-domain diversity, not merely a deploy button. The recurring cost buys patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Coolify
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosting platform for applications, databases, and services.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.desc: One-server container hosting with Git deploys, TLS, logs, limits, and a dashboard you can understand.

facts.install: Coolify Cloud signup or one-line install script on a fresh Linux server
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted control data is in an internal PostgreSQL container; deployed apps and databases remain in Docker containers, volumes, and configuration on the user's servers
facts.gapVsPaid: Coolify gives one server a capable deployment control plane, but it cannot reproduce Fly.io's multi-region edge placement, Anycast networking, or provider-operated global infrastructure.
facts.setupBlocker: A VPS with root SSH access, open ports, DNS, and responsibility for server patching and application-data backups

alternatives.name: Dokku
alternatives.desc: The original tiny Heroku-on-one-box; excellent once you are comfortable treating a server like a pet.

facts.install: Bootstrap script on a fresh supported Ubuntu or Debian VM, then add an SSH key and domain
facts.dataFormat: Application images, configuration, logs, and persistent Docker volumes live on the user's server; service data lives in installed database-plugin volumes
facts.gapVsPaid: Dokku is excellent on one box, but its CLI-first, single-host model lacks Fly.io's global regions, edge networking, and managed operational surface.
facts.setupBlocker: A fresh Linux VM, sudo/SSH competence, DNS, and command-line-only administration

alternatives.name: Dokploy
alternatives.desc: A newer self-hosted PaaS for apps and databases, with previews, TLS, logs, and backups in the same control plane.

facts.install: Dokploy Cloud signup or one-line install script on a Linux VPS
facts.dataFormat: Dokploy metadata is stored in PostgreSQL; application and database data lives in Docker named volumes or bind mounts on the deployment servers, with optional S3 backups
facts.gapVsPaid: Dokploy brings apps, databases, previews, and backups to your own servers, but global placement, Anycast networking, and provider-managed capacity are not included.
facts.setupBlocker: A VPS with at least 2 GB RAM, free ports 80/443/3000, DNS, and ongoing Docker/server administration

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Usage based plan and a single-server personal platform DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Fly.io in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a small Go control plane; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: deploy one container on a user-owned server, route domains, retain logs, perform backups, and expose operational limits clearly.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept a Git repository or container image and one explicit Dockerfile-based build path.
Implement applications, environments, secrets, domains, health checks, and rolling container replacement.
Use Caddy for automatic TLS and route only to healthy local containers.
Capture bounded build and runtime logs and expose restart, rollback, and redeploy actions.
Back up PostgreSQL metadata and document backups for each deployed application's data volumes.
Add host metrics, disk alerts, update instructions, disaster recovery, and a prominent single-server warning.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-region or serverless infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out managed data stores and global edge delivery.
Deliberately leave out DDoS response, compliance, and guaranteed uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
